column2: Rosenberg and Bill become friends after seeing a great deal of each other in the summer of 1952; Rosenberg plays the provocateur, Bill tosses out cryptic remarks to be decoded; the two couples are bound by a shared dislike of Lee Krasner, then on a fierce and harrowing crusade to promote her husband and crush any rival. In private, Bill made fun of Rosenberg's theories.

A refined dinner at the home of the German intellectual Fritz Hensler; he locks up the liquor brought by the guests, Kline forces the cabinet and redistributes the bottles; the leg of lamb is eaten amid an uproar worthy of the Cedar Tavern; at dawn, with the question of beds unresolved, Elaine announces that she will walk back to New York and limps off in her cast, forcing Bill to go after her. Four cars to carry the guests; bottles of Scotch, gin, and vodka; German Moselle wine (poured into the plants or spilled on the floor, depending on the version); leg of lamb; Elaine in a leg cast; martinis Consequences: The end of the elegant dinner Hensler had wanted; Elaine would later say she was ashamed of the artists' behavior

Met at the Cedar Tavern, the commercial artist Joan Ward becomes the mistress of Bill, who moves to the top floor of 88 East 10th Street, between 3rd and 4th Avenues; she lives next door. Consequences: De facto separation of the couple during the year of the Women

Elaine goes with artist friends to the four-day festival: Cunningham choreographs Stravinsky's Les Noces and Pierre Schaeffer's Symphonie pour un homme seul; Bernstein conducts Blitzstein's adaptation of The Threepenny Opera and premieres his own opera Trouble in Tahiti; Elaine would later cryptically cite this Threepenny Opera as an explanation for some of her mother's beliefs.
In the fall of 1952, Bill moves to 88 East 10th Street, which becomes the heart of an unofficial artists' colony and attracts daring galleries. Consequences: A new hub of the art scene.

A party at Fritz Hensler's (described as a philosophy professor by Lionel Abel and as a sociologist by Edvard Lieber), when Elaine's leg was still in a cast; Lieber dates it to July 1951 from Elaine's recollections, but since the accident dates from November 1951, the author proposes the spring of 1952. A later visit to Hensler's took place in February 1954. A cast on her leg; diverging accounts by Abel (Intellectual Follies, 215-16) and Lieber

Anni takes Kubler's course on pre-Columbian art and chooses as her research the reconstruction of the Andean weavers' techniques for the very wide pieces of ancient Nazca; she draws the expert Junius Bird into a debate (letter of April 21, 1952). The essay will appear as “A Structural Process in Weaving” in On Designing (1959). Letter to Bird, April 21, 1952 Consequences: Publication in On Designing

Cruz's controversial resignation allows Piwonka to take over Composición Pura (called Plástica), closer to the Bauhaus model, then standardized through Albers's work in Chile from 1953. Piwonka will direct it until 1967, when it is replaced by Octavio Sotomayor's Taller de Arquitectura. Consequences: The model of the Preliminary Course passes to the PUC schools of Art and Design

At the start of his deanship (1952-1967), Sergio Larraín asks Emilio Duhart to contact a teacher of international standing to direct, for a time, the course in Composición Pre-Arquitectónica taught by Piwonka. Consequences: Albers arrives in Chile in June 1953

Anni takes George Kubler's class on pre-Columbian art; her research concerns the reconstruction of the Andean weavers' techniques for the very wide fabrics of ancient Nazca; she debates by letter with the textile expert Junius Bird of the Museum of Natural History in New York. Letter to Bird of April 21, 1952: her speculations may seem “far-fetched to non-weavers” Consequences: Research published as “A Structural Process in Weaving” in On Designing (1959)

Cruz's disputed resignation allows Piwonka to take over Pure Composition, renamed Plastic Art, closer to the Bauhaus model; Piwonka will teach it until 1967, when Octavio Sotomayor's Architecture Workshop replaces it. Consequences: The course is standardized after 1953 under the influence of Albers's work in Chile.

Having become dean of the PUC's school of architecture and fine arts (1952-67), Sergio Larrain entrusts Emilio Duhart, one of the most important Chilean modern architects, with finding a teacher of international standing for the course in Pure Composition then taught by Piwonka. Consequences: Duhart approaches Josef Albers.
Josef teaches at the University of Havana (February 9-17); summer in Mexico, the Maya ruins of Yucatán; Anni begins designing for Knoll.

A visit to Nell to escape the heat of Arlington, Virginia; the summer institute is in session: Olson the giant, Cage's lecture on Zen Buddhism, Kline's paintings, the Weinribs' stoneware; the lake still polluted, daily swims at the North Fork swimming hole, where they meet Rauschenberg and Thiel, all admiring the smooth pebbles on the bank. Consequences: Last sight of the college in operation.

Max Dehn dies while Dawson is in military service. He is buried among the rhododendrons below the reservoir. Grave: rhododendrons below the reservoir. Consequences: A flash-forward by Dawson, then in the army.

On a cool, softly misty fall morning, Dawson, sitting on the rocks at the summit, hears a muffled rustling: Max Dehn appears on the path near the barbed wire that Dawson had helped string. Hollow but rosy cheeks, deep and very bright eyes, white hair in the wind, collar half turned up, slightly stooped. They exchange a smile and a murmured hello; the small bent figure passes and disappears into the fog. Consequences: Shortly before Dawson was drafted, Dehn was visibly fading away.

After politely asking to take Branwen, aged two and a half, promising to show her the wildflowers, Dehn walked hand in hand with her, his white hair shining in the sun, for an hour on the wooded slope; they came back delighted with each other and he bowed ceremoniously to her. A few days later, a hearse came early in the morning to load his body in the clearing. 2½ years old; white hair in the sun; an hour's walk; a hearse in the early morning Consequences: Dehn's death

The academic dean, Worth Howard, interviewed them; they showed him around the college and regaled him with exaggerated stories about the school. Fearing they had ruined their chances, they were hired: Howard reportedly told the trustees that having survived BMC and been able to laugh about it, they were tough enough for Egypt. Howard's remark to the trustees, as reported Consequences: The couple leaves for Cairo

Back as Olson had ordered, she shows him her journal; a few days of glory in which she is the star of the workshop, now down to six students. The first week, Olson hovers over them, gliding behind his thick glasses, his finger on a pared-down line of the journal: “I pointed westward, towards his grave” (about her father). Six students; thick glasses; the line about her father's grave Consequences: “Si, si, girl! That's space!”, Olson triumphant

Three highly autobiographical stories about her childhood, following Olson's precept to write from the center, win her the annual Creative Writing Award given to a senior at Barnard. $500, a tidy sum for the time Consequences: Olson's jealousy and hostility toward the judges from New York publishing houses

Furious at the New York prizes, Olson follows up with a new tutorial, shouting that she is still writing conservative junk, that she must stick to a journal, and above all not try to publish anything for ten years. The giant walrus rises from his chair, his six feet seven unfolded. Six feet seven; shouting; forbidden to publish for ten years Consequences: A second censor; she obeys and keeps her journal for years

Kline succeeds Jack Tworkov, the guest artist for June, whose intellectual and learned approach to contemporary art contrasted with the smiling generosity of Kline, who was in no way the professor and had no idea how to teach. Tworkov invited in June; learned versus generous Consequences: A very positive impact on the community

At the end of the summer, Olson suggests that McGee stay for the fall and winter; McGee, already enrolled in graduate school at Indiana University, would accept if the college could get him a master's degree. Olson rubs his chin and looks at him with his enormous eyes: “Okay”; he calls the Board of Fellows together. The board deliberates for the better part of a morning and concludes that even with all its imagination, the college cannot pull off this feat. A morning of deliberation; a master's degree impossible, though a BA was possible Consequences: The effort and the goodwill remain memorable for McGee

McGee's open-air studio is just below Wolpe's apartment in the Studies Building; the poorly insulated floors subject him to the composer's moods and rages. Wolpe, a strong, fiery European personality, becomes for many “our Far-out Beethoven”: warm toward Lou Harrison, distant toward John Cage, the moodiest and most volatile member of that summer's faculty. Uninsulated floors; the nickname “Far-out Beethoven”

Rauschenberg is the first person McGee and his wife Marty meet on arriving; tall and imposing, he immediately offers a hand unloading the old '39 Ford. He spots a bundle of small canvases whose compositions have been covered with zinc white (still faintly visible underneath) and is enthusiastic: “This is really an interesting painting.” 1939 Ford; small format; zinc white; gestures at arm's length Consequences: McGee, unsettled, no longer knows what to paint on these canvases

Adams, an anthropologist and art lover struggling with a canvas, goes to knock at Rauschenberg's door at night; when the porch light comes on, he discovers to his horror that he has stepped on a canvas laid out to dry; the footprints go into the paint. An unlit porch; a canvas laid out on the porch floor Consequences: For the witness, this incident sums up the avant-garde nature of academic life at BMC

Olson's scheme to replace the basic curriculum with institutes: the interaction of leading professionals, as in the summer sessions. Five eight-week institutes planned: crafts; theater bringing together actors, dancers, writers, musicians, and painters (Boris Aronson considered to lead it); the new sciences of man (Christopher Hawkes, from England, considered); natural sciences with an emphasis on ecology; the arts in summer. The remaining academics (except Flola Shepard) lose all hope; Sprague denounces a community like a bag of jumping beans, in intellectual, moral, and physical disintegration. 5 institutes, 8 weeks each Consequences: The departure of the last academics, Sprague included

Back from her year's leave, she despises Olson and soon judges it impossible to dislodge him; the catalog nonetheless credits her with nine courses, from introductory chemistry to atomic physics. 9 courses listed under her name

A truncated three-week seminar on archaeology and mythology: Olson, Braidwood (the excavator of Jarmo), and Maria von Franz, Jung's associate. Jung himself had been invited and had proposed von Franz, already on a lecture tour.
The English anthropologist would have come, but required, as a precondition, that the college also pay his girlfriend's travel, which the community could not afford.

A few months before the institute, they accept the post that all the students at Alfred University had turned down, indignant at the $80 a month. They discover the workshop built by Bob Turner, unused since he left but in perfect condition. Salary: $80 a month; a workshop in a flat field near the Studies Building, large windows on the valley, the best kiln one could dream of, a fully equipped studio. Consequences: A compromise: “potters-in-residence,” but not members of the faculty the first year; the kiln self-supporting (purchases and receipts kept).

Karnes has few students; Mary Caroline Richards works intensively with the couple. Some people scorn her pots as not rough, real, or natural enough, because she sells in shops in Asheville and New York. After Thanksgiving dinner, people pile turkey bones in Karnes's dishes to show their contempt (as told by Remy Charlip).

He had already come in 1948-1949 to follow Sue Weil, then considered a more serious painter than he was; Albers had found him frivolous and told him he had nothing to teach him. In 1952, married to Sue, he returns after the shock of his white canvases at the Betty Parsons Gallery. In 1948-1949: imaginative costumes, dye baths cooking on the kitchen stove, purple underwear coming out of them. Consequences: With Cage and Cunningham, and the help of David Tudor, he pursues explorations of form that will mark mixed-media theater.
Sexual paths explored that summer disconcert Olson, Fiore, and Rice, men who share a stereotyped, almost truck-driver view of masculinity.

Lou Harrison, a Guggenheim fellow for 1952-1953, persuades Wolpe, tired of teaching, to replace him. Wolpe, 50, teaches composition; his wife, the poet Hilda Morley, teaches literature and Hebrew. Wolpe and Olson, both dynamic, take to each other immediately; the climate suits the new direction of his music. Wolpe had known Jalowetz in Germany, had studied with Webern, and had taught at the Philadelphia Musical Academy (where David Tudor was his student). Consequences: Wolpe decides to stay after 1953, to Harrison's great regret; Cage sees it as a usurpation.

Invited to teach composition (which flatters him; no other school would have dreamed of it), Cage announces that he will teach not the students' work but his own, with them as apprentices making the “Williams Mix.” Not one student signs up; he gives up all organized teaching and simply becomes the music students' friend. Long sessions of discussion and strip poker with the music students. Consequences: No formal class; the nightly reading of Huang Po as the only class.

A complete reading of the first edition of Huang Po's Doctrine of Universal Mind (notes, preface, everything), before 20 to 30 people from a community swollen to about 70 for the summer. Several listeners act out the dialogue in which the master insults the pupil. Consequences: A profound effect, notably on a Korean War veteran at the end of his rope and on another student at a perplexing point in his life.

Cage uses chance operations exclusively and composes the “Williams Mix” on magnetic tape, funded by Paul and Vera Williams, benefactors of the college. Paul Williams also supported David Tudor and the Living Theatre early on, always without conditions, and magnificently.

Cage reads aloud the Zen text of Huang Po, which he considers the essential text, before twenty to thirty people; several listeners help him, notably by acting out the dialogue section in which the master insults the pupil. 20 to 30 listeners from a community of about 70 people for the summer session Consequences: A profound effect on a Korean War veteran at the end of his rope and on a student at a bewildering turning point in his life

Cage, with Tudor, devises a 45-minute theatrical event (the length of the time brackets he draws on paper) in which each guest freely fills his or her slot: poetry readings (Olson, M.C. Richards), paintings and records (Rauschenberg), piano (Tudor), dance (Cunningham). The audience, seated in the center in four sections divided by diagonals, finds an empty white cup on each chair; coffee is poured into the cups at the end, including those used as ashtrays. 45 minutes of planned time brackets; empty white cups on the seats; coffee poured at the end; screaming children; barking dogs Consequences: The event will be considered the prehistoric forerunner of the happenings of the 1960s (Allan Kaprow)
The composer Stefan Wolpe, furious at the event, gets up and leaves in the middle of the performance.

According to Weinrib, Mrs. Jalowetz, a beautiful woman from the radical German tradition (Schoenberg), repeats like an incantation “Deep in the middle ages”; Olson, sitting next to her, stays noncommittal, playing it cool, before the poem he had written in advance and distributed to the audience. Olson had written the poem in fragments and handed out the lines to spectators, who stood up in turn

A simultaneous performance whose elements are poorly reconstructed: a stepladder or lectern (M.C. Richards was on a horse or in a basket, so probably Rauschenberg or Olson was on it; Olson perhaps went down into the audience after his reading); Rauschenberg showed something of his own (black or white canvases) as backdrop or foreground; a phonograph with records from the 1920s-30s or by Édith Piaf; the audience in the center (triangles, squares, or undivided) with aisles in which Merce danced, followed by a dog, barking or silent; Cage read something (one account says Emerson and Thoreau); Tudor played something (perhaps Cunningham himself played); projections (slides, films, montages, painted glass). Everyone loved it except Wolpe and Johanna Jalowetz (who at least liked the participants). Considered possibly the very first “multimedia” event. Stepladder/lectern, horse, basket, phonograph, records from the 1920s-30s or Piaf, dog, slides or painted glass, Rauschenberg's black or white canvases Consequences: Considered in retrospect the first multimedia event; foundational material for Cunningham, Cage, Rauschenberg, and Tudor.

Kline spent most of the summer at the college; everyone loved him and he loved Black Mountain, but he worried that the young people were learning nothing that would help them earn a living as painters or writers. Before an exhibition of paintings, he said that they must be great paintings because he felt absolutely “helpless” or “hopeless” (Cage no longer remembers which word). A remark before an exhibition of paintings

Cunningham places this episode perhaps the previous summer: Olson decided to study dance, came regularly, and worked hard, at considerable physical risk; he told Cunningham he did not have to watch him if he did not want to. Cunningham grimaced in incomprehension at first (he was actually concentrating) and ended up getting this physical experience. Cunningham compares him to a “light walrus”
Too busy to have an operation, he went on a diet and ran around pressing an ice bag to his stomach whenever the pain came. By 1953 he was in excellent physical shape. Ice bag on the stomach

A (failed) attempt to revive Forbes's interest: Huss describes two impulses, the rigidity of control among those who feared that irrationality would dominate, and the impulse toward abolishing all limits in a group responding blindly to the philosophy of sensation; on both sides, incurable romantics reacting rather than acting.

The farm in good shape after Ray Trayer's departure, plans to extend the land under Doyle Jones; $5,000 borrowed from Paul Williams for the beef herd, $5,000 more for scholarships and operations; the new science building ($6,000 given by Forbes) remains unfinished, since the students had not been able to build as well as they designed, and Dan Rice came back with a small crew to finish it; five acres sold to a neighbor; a new attempt at accreditation (enrollment of 35 in 1952, a low point); still talk of a rector or chief administrator; the Community Council (flourishing under Wallen) is revived. $5,000 (herd) + $5,000 (scholarships/operations), $6,000 (Forbes, science), 35 students, 5 acres sold Consequences: Nearly all these projects will fail; by the end of 1953 the community has shrunk.

Many felt as early as 1952 that the physical (not spiritual) decay was well advanced, but cared little: Olson argued that this impoverished atmosphere is the only one favorable to living and working, and that the place's second surge was now in full swing.

An alumnus from the 1930s comes back to supervise a reorganized work program; nine special work scholarships are created, allowing some students to put in up to thirty hours of labor a week. The kibbutz spirit flares up, but briefly. 9 special scholarships; a maximum of 30 hours of work a week Consequences: Quick discontent: the scholarship holders feel they lack time for classes and denounce unfair distinctions among students, contrary to the community philosophy.

The council, re-formed, lasts about five months and vigorously debates trivial matters: dog droppings in the Studies Building; replacing Fielding Dawson on the heating detail (the only warm nights being those of Olson's writing classes, of which Dawson was a fervent member); scribbling on the bulletin board; failing the state health inspections (requirements: bottling the farm's grade A milk, rebuilding the Studies Building's sewer line), and whether to look clean or be clean; Paul Goodman's dog Tinkerbelle, abandoned a year earlier with a false promise of monthly money, which Tim La Farge has to go on feeding; the noise of recorders in the Studies Building, without even the consolation of noting any progress; students dressed as cowboys firing imaginary shots at the screen of the local movie theater. Goodman's broken promise: monthly money for the dog's food, a year without payment Consequences: At the end of 1952, a one-sentence declaration: the council has no positive function that the Board, the work committee, or the community cannot take on; “We therefore resign.”

Rumaker drops his knife into the conveyor, stopping the machinery with a horrible screech; Doyle then puts him in the silo, where he has to tramp down the silage by jumping with another student while the corn rises higher and higher; Rumaker is terrified of heights. He climbs down by the metal rungs set into the silo's concrete. Knife dropped into the conveyor, silage blown by the fan into the top of the silo, metal rungs in slots in the concrete Consequences: Judged lacking in sturdiness, he is transferred to the kitchen: dishes, scrubbing, and mopping floors seven days a week.

Fuller relates that, to counter Olson, Natasha suggested he take over the leadership of the college; Dan Rice asserts that Natasha wanted to replace Olson and, having failed, left in a rage. Consequences: Goldowski leaves in a fit of temper

The day before the evening at the Olsons', the group visits Thomas Wolfe's childhood home, which feeds Rumaker's literary intoxication with the region. The “Old Kentucky Home” house, connected with Look Homeward, Angel Consequences: Strengthens Rumaker's desire to live in these mountains

Charles, a fast driver with one hand resting on the wheel, talks easily over his shoulder; Rumaker, in the back next to Mary Ann, is dazzled by the enormous golden moon rising above the black hills. A convertible with the top down, 12 miles to Asheville, a full moon, golden light, then pale blue Consequences: Rumaker falls in love with the valley and with the Olsons

Back late, Olson leafs through the metrical poems without comment and tosses them aside like wasted paper, but reads the story about an abortion with grunts of interest and seriously encourages Rumaker to apply. Manuscripts taken out of an old suitcase lent by his mother; tea made by Olson in the small kitchen Consequences: Rumaker decides to apply to BMC

Rumaker says he can pay only a fraction of the $1,600 annual fees; Olson directs him to the formal application for a work scholarship, to be made to Connie, the registrar: at least four hours of work a day on the farm or in the kitchen in exchange for tuition and board; a decision by the committee of teachers and students at the end of August or in early September. $1,600 a year, at least 4 hours a day, decision at the end of August or in early September Consequences: Rumaker's way into BMC opens

Mary Ann decides to continue at Moore Institute, hoping to come for a summer session (she will come the following summer for photography). Marge, exhausted and irritated at driving alone, drops Mary Ann at home, then the group arrives unannounced at Rumaker's mother's house. Marge refuses to let Roger drive despite his license Consequences: Olson seems disappointed by Mary Ann's refusal

Arrival around midafternoon while his father is at work at the shipyards; his mother, caught off guard, apologizes for her housedress and the state of the house; Rumaker is ashamed of the worn linoleum and of his mother, then ashamed of being ashamed; he leaves before his father comes home. No telephone at his parents'; a house where eleven people lived crowded together; his mother schooled only through the fifth grade, never having gone farther than across the river from South Philly Consequences: Rumaker takes his things and leaves, relieved

Every evening at the concerts in the Amphitheater, Rumaker spots a young blond man in a navy blazer with gold buttons, always alone at the same ramp entrance, and develops a violent but mute passion, never daring to approach. A navy blazer with gold buttons, a blond crew cut, a few ramps away Consequences: He embodies everything Rumaker thinks he wants to be: handsome, rich, self-assured, outwardly heterosexual

Rumaker loses his gay virginity with a middle-aged geometry teacher, stiff and closed, in the attic room the man rents every season. He gets into bed in his underpants, which amuses Wood; afterward, Rumaker knows that this is more right for him than it was with his high school girlfriend. Underpants (“jockeys”), attic room, seasonal rental Consequences: Confirmation of his identity; entry into the Chautauqua homosexual network through “Woody”

Through Woody, Rumaker meets regulars, young and old, who come every season to spot new boys, bring them out, and then pass them along to one another for further erotic education. Ritual questions: “Did you bring him out?” / “Remember you owe me one” Consequences: Rumaker confirms that Roger was right: Chautauqua is crawling with homosexuals

Rumaker discovers William Carlos Williams's stories in Make Light of It, then, after a special request and a lie about his age (he is not yet 21), Proust (Sodom and Gomorrah), Joyce (Ulysses), and Faulkner (Light in August), locked away behind brown curtains in the basement. The librarian's big ring of keys; a solid wooden double-doored cabinet; “such books are kept out of sight” Consequences: A revelation: he had not known one was allowed to write like that

After a particularly dull session, Hilda confidentially asks Rumaker how to revive interest, then, without waiting for the answer: “Tea! Yes! I'll serve tea!”. She brings a hot plate from Black Dwarf; Rumaker brings tea bags, lemon slices, and cups from the kitchen. Hot plate, tea bags, lemon, cups Consequences: A pleasant break, but with no effect; after a last class on Henry James's stories, Hilda disappears from the classrooms (except for posing nude in Esteban Vicente's drawing class at the 1953 Summer Institute)
Wes casts Fee in Brecht's Mother Courage and Her Children; Fee launches into fierce arguments about how to play, or not play, the part.

Over Ballantine ales at Ma Peak's tavern on the highway, Cynthia draws on the back of a coaster the shapes Virginia has designed for several of her pots: all distinctly phallic. Ballantine ales, a beer coaster

After lunch, Virginia photographs Rumaker as he chatters with nervous energy; she calmly rewinds her film and says in her slow baby voice: “You exaggerate everything”. Pale blue-rimmed glasses Consequences: The remark offends and then instructs Rumaker: good liars make good writers; the lie of the imagination creates the truth of the real
One day Huss sends the drama class away because the students had not yet thought about what they were doing.

After lunch, Virginia takes a photograph of Rumaker as he chatters with nervous energy; she quietly rewinds her film and tells him he exaggerates everything, which silences him and then makes him think. Pale blue-rimmed glasses, a slow baby-talk voice Consequences: Rumaker draws from it a writer's motto: good liars make good writers

Judging the science building that the students built at the top of the slope above Lake Eden to be dangerous, she teaches physics in the hall of Meadows Inn, where she lives with Eric Renner. About six students lying on pallets covered with throws, a huge roaring fireplace, small glasses of Grand Marnier on crisp fall mornings, two-hour classes

Several mornings a week at 10 a.m. sharp, a one-hour lesson: the first half campus gossip (who is sleeping with whom) with questions in English, the second half reading aloud translations from an old textbook containing Jules Verne's Around the World in Eighty Days; Madame often dozes off, then murmurs “très bien.” Six vicious stray dogs, a cup of tea, “Allez, allez”, “Szlence!”, a bony finger pointed at the corner, the textbook probably brought over in the hatbox Consequences: Rumaker learns a nineteenth-century French with a White Russian accent, incomprehensible to others

The former writing students mill around waiting for Olson; a few students, including Mary and Joe Fiore, collect a hundred dollars as an extra salary to bring him back to the cash-strapped college. $100, a sum that went a long way at the time
Olson stays away, holed up with his family in the apartment of the wealthy patron and Black Sun Press publisher Caresse Crosby. Consequences: Rumaker's bitterness, a feeling of wasting his time

He paints three walls of his cubicle (the door wall being frosted glass) white, black, and bright yellow, in imitation of the abstract paintings at the college, with cheap paint bought from Carroll. White, black, and yellow walls; frosted glass; hard on astigmatism, in the manner of Albers and Kline

Worried that the students are isolating themselves, Mary organizes charming late-afternoon teas with plates of butter cookies she bakes herself in the college kitchen. Plates of homemade butter cookies Consequences: The newcomers socialize

At Mary's suggestion, a shy Rumaker organizes a reading: Oppenheimer reads poems by William Carlos Williams, Dan Rice an essay on architecture, Ed Stresino some of Pound's Cantos in a deep, stentorian voice. Consequences: It helped, but something was missing without Olson

On the way to BMC, Stresino stops to visit Pound, incarcerated for his treasonous broadcasts from Mussolini's Italy; Jonathan Williams, a visitor at the same time, finds the poet surrounded by sinister, fascist-looking Jesuit priests. Psychiatric hospital

The Fiores pile students into their Jeep station wagon for the classic afternoon screenings at the Pack Library; there Rumaker discovers Marlene Dietrich in The Blue Angel and Buster Keaton's The General, which bowl him over. Jeep station wagon; films: The Blue Angel, The General

Coming back late from a movie, they pick up a tall, gangly man in overalls and a faded plaid shirt, carrying a baby in his arms; he says only “Much obliged,” stiff and mute, and gets out at the road leading up to the college. “Much obliged,” his only words; a baby in his arms Consequences: Mary murmurs that there must be trouble at home, troubled by a child out so late

For the silage of several tons of cornstalks, neighboring farmers come to help; Doyle pushes the pace at dusk, and Rumaker can no longer cut the twine with his pocketknife on the sped-up conveyor (the accident follows, beyond the passage). Tractor and trailer, metal belt, pocketknives, chopper, blowing into the concrete silo through a side slot, Ben (14, a stutterer) and a student tramping down the silage and closing it off with boards, the sun sinking toward the mountains Consequences: A stupid accident gets Rumaker sent off the farm
The morning after the silo episode, Rumaker asks Hazel Frieda Larsen whether he might not be better employed in the kitchen. Consequences: He then works in the kitchen and the dining hall

Pat Nelson gets a jaywalking ticket in Asheville and is baffled by the policeman's insistence, used as she is to the freedom of Black Mountain; she does not understand the logic of city law and reports on it angrily back on campus.

One evening Dorothy, an expert, sets out to hypnotize Rumaker, sitting on his bed, in front of Pat and a few onlookers; at the repeated phrases of her silky voice, rings of light pass through Rumaker's eyes; on the verge of losing consciousness, he pulls himself up by an effort of will and wakes, trembling for several minutes; Dorothy checks that he is all right, calms him, laughs her good-natured laugh (she admits he is her first failure), and exclaims, delighted: “But I almost gotcha!”. The experiment was not repeated. A bed, an upstairs back room; a body trembling for minutes

Dorothy, lively and sociable, starts spending time with Tommy, a taciturn night owl, in his cluttered study; she adopts his inverted rhythm (sleeping by day, working by night), they are heard laughing behind the closed door, a DO NOT DISTURB sign on the knob; she seems more radiant than ever, he contentedly calm; they are seldom seen together, sometimes in the two-seater MG (before the accident) on errands in Buncombe County. Sign printed by Tommy; two-seater MG Consequences: Quiet jealousy from Pat and Rumaker, deprived of Dorothy.

Harrison sometimes disappeared for days at the Gatehouse near the county road, getting high on pots of tea brewed on a hot plate and composing on a battered old upright piano, even sleeping there; when he reappeared, he would tell about it all, laughing, his face flushed and his eyes bright; he also worked at the Music House in the middle of the woods. Hot plate, pot after pot of tea, an old upright piano

On Sunday evenings, with the cooks off, Nell Rice would invite two or three new students to eat their cheese and Malrey's homemade bread, with tea or coffee and sometimes a dessert, to get acquainted, exchange ideas, and talk about the library. Cheese, Malrey's homemade bread, tea or coffee, dessert; Sunday evening

In the fall of 1952, Wes Huss held auditions and early rehearsals in the hall of Roadside (where he lives upstairs with Bea and their baby David), then the company rehearsed for weeks at the end of the dining hall in front of the huge fieldstone fireplace; a spare, dark set with no flats, platforms on several levels marking the places, austere lighting; severely black costumes; Bea played the Mother of the Bridegroom, played by Rumaker; Rumaker suspects he was cast to awaken a latent heterosexuality in him. Platforms, no stage; fieldstone fireplace; black costumes; their son David, a toddler

After slipping away, Rumaker is checking his stage makeup (“pancake makeup”) in the restroom mirrors when Wes Huss appears in the doorway: everyone is waiting for him; his entrance was due long ago. Huss, calm and even, tells him to save his excuses for later; they race down the stairs and back across the road; Rumaker slips in through the side doors of the dining hall and climbs onto his assigned platform while the rest of the cast, frozen in their formal poses, stares at him. Mirrors above the sinks, pancake makeup, assigned platform, side doors of the dining hall Consequences: Huss denies him any immediate excuse; Rumaker's embarrassment before the cast

In early winter 1952, with so few students on campus, walking into the dining hall for dinner and hearing three or four students play Bach, pitch-perfect, on recorders, gathered regularly by the dark windows overlooking the even darker Lake Eden. Consequences: A luminous comfort of the spirit in the depopulated college

In winter, coffee is a comfort: when the kitchen is closed and the urns are empty, one boils water in a big open pot, throws in a lot of coffee, lets it boil a few minutes, sprinkles in cold water and raps the pot hard to settle the grounds, and waits a minute or two before serving. Some swear it is better than Cornelia's urn coffee, delicious as that is. Cynthia Homire taught Rumaker the recipe. A big open pot, plenty of coffee, a sprinkling of cold water, grounds at the bottom Consequences: Rumaker sees it as part of his education at the college, as important as a clear sentence or a clean brushstroke

A few weeks after Meadows Inn, Rumaker discovers by chance that Merrill is partially deaf, like his own older brother Bill. Consequences: Explains Merrill's head tilted to listen; a link with Rumaker's childhood

After his turn at the dinner dishes, Rumaker goes in to shower and finds the veteran, back from an afternoon at the farm, standing stark naked under the bare bulbs by the shower stalls, drying himself. Thin, wavy red hair with tips burnished copper by the sun in the fields, sunburned skin, muscular, freckled shoulders, a lean, wiry body. It is Saturday night: he is clearly getting ready to go to Asheville. Rumaker, paralyzed by his beauty and fearful of the college's mores, dares not say anything and takes refuge in a shower stall. Bare bulbs, the redness of hair and shoulders, the dormitory's spring mattresses, 20 feet between their beds, a corner always as neat as in the army Consequences: The image haunts Rumaker for days and weeks; he is relieved when the man leaves the college

Despite his loyal friendship with his comrade and their shared interest in music, he does not stay long: Rumaker supposes he felt out of place or that loneliness was eating at him (he complained, under his breath, about the lack of women and drove to Asheville on Saturday nights). Consequences: Relief for Rumaker, uncomfortable in his presence since the shower scene

Raiding the freezer (cheese from Sunday lunch, leftover cornbread, milk) was against one of the college's few rules (along with the ban on hopping freight trains and owning guns), but almost everyone did it; a sturdier padlock was put on the freezer door, which Tommy Jackson, whom Rumaker suspects of a criminal bent, soon knew how to open. A reinforced padlock, cheese, cornbread, milk, Malrey Few's old coal stove converted to oil
After Cissy's brief stay with the painter and farmhand Don Jones in his room at North Lodge, she has moved back in with Joel at Last Chance, to the relief of some.

Rumaker discovers Williams's stories in Make Light of It at the Jamestown library: Williams lets him see that one can write a new kind of story in idiomatic American speech. Consequences: He reads all the Williams he can find in the Black Mountain library

Rosenberg publishes his founding article describing Action Painting: the canvas as an arena in which to act rather than a space in which to reproduce; “What was to go on the canvas was not a picture but an event.” Famous formula: the canvas as an “arena in which to act”. Consequences: An article read as a manifesto, setting de Kooning on a throne and attacking Clement Greenberg.

Three months after Rosenberg's article, Hess publishes his article with photographs by Rudy Burckhardt, describing how de Kooning works on a Woman painting and building up the portrait of the artist as hero. A painting photographed at several stages, seen as the stages of a journey; the Woman's smile compared to the Greek kouros and the medieval Virgin. Consequences: Consecrates de Kooning in the media alongside Rosenberg's article.

Begun in mutual esteem in the 1930s, the relationship degenerates into hostility after Pollock's rise to fame: jealousy over magazine coverage, competition over sale prices; each wife campaigns to crown her husband; Greenberg and Rosenberg wage the war of words. If one sold a canvas, the other had to sell for more; de Kooning would later say that Pollock's painting was “like chain-smoking”. Consequences: The question of who was better, Jackson or Bill, goes on after Pollock's death in 1956.

At a drunken party, Pollock, already depressed, interrupts Harold's declamations with furious remarks; Harold puts him down and orders him to go to bed, and Jackson obeys; Lee flies into a blind rage, convinced that Harold set it up to humiliate Jackson. Pollock's remarks: “What a lot of shit”, “horse piss” Consequences: The beginning of the public competition between the two painters, according to Naifeh and Smith
